questions.question: Consider the matrix \[M = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 0 \\ -1 & a & b \end{bmatrix}\]. Which of the following options is/ are TRUE if \(\det (M) \neq 0\)?
questions.explanation:
Given matrix \[M = egin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 3 & 0 \ -1 & a & b \end{bmatrix}\]. \[\det(M) = 2(3b - 0) - 1(b - 0) + 1(a - (-3))\] \[\det(M) = 6b - b + a + 3\] \[\det(M) = 5b + a + 3\] For the matrix to be non-singular, we must have: \[5b + a + 3 eq 0\] Now we check each option:
  • Option (A): \(a = -\dfrac{1}{2}, b = -\dfrac{1}{2}\) \[5\left(-\dfrac{1}{2} ight) + \left(-\dfrac{1}{2} ight) + 3 = -\dfrac{5}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} + 3 = -3 + 3 = 0\] This makes \(\det(M) = 0\), so it is FALSE.
  • Option (B): \(a = \dfrac{1}{2}, b = \dfrac{1}{2}\) \[5\left(\dfrac{1}{2} ight) + \dfrac{1}{2} + 3 = 3 + 3 = 6 eq 0\] This is TRUE.
  • Option (C): \(a = -3, b = 0\) \[5(0) + (-3) + 3 = 0\] This makes \(\det(M) = 0\), so it is FALSE.
  • Option (D): \(a = \dfrac{1}{2}, b = -3\) \[5(-3) + \dfrac{1}{2} + 3 = -15 + 3.5 = -11.5 eq 0\] This is TRUE.
\[ oxed{ ext{(B) $a = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $b = \dfrac{1}{2}$, (D) $a = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $b = -3$}}\]
Key points
  • A matrix \(M\) is non-singular if and only if \(\det(M) eq 0\).
  • The determinant of a \(3 imes 3\) matrix \(A = [a_{ij}]\) can be found using Laplace expansion: \(\det(A) = \sum_{j=1}^{3} (-1)^{i+j} a_{ij} M_{ij}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Ensure correct sign convention (\(+ - +\)) when expanding the determinant.
  • Do not confuse the condition \(\det(M) eq 0\) (invertible) with \(\det(M) = 0\) (singular).

questions.question: Consider the square region \(R\) in the \(X\)-\(Y\) plane as shown with the dark shading in the Figure. The value of \(\iint\limits_{R} (x^2 + y^2 - 1) \, dx \, dy\) is . (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation:
The given integral over the square region \(R\) is: \[I = \iint\limits_{R} (x^2 + y^2 - 1) \, dx \, dy\] Separating the integral into two parts: \[I = \iint\limits_{R} (x^2 + y^2) \, dx \, dy - \iint\limits_{R} 1 \, dy \, dx\] \[I = I_1 - I_2\] For \(I_1\), considering the symmetry of the region \(R\) across the \(x\)-axis and splitting it at \(x = 1\): \[I_1 = \int_{0}^{1} \int_{-x}^{x} (x^2 + y^2) \, dy \, dx + \int_{1}^{2} \int_{-(2-x)}^{(2-x)} (x^2 + y^2) \, dy \, dx\] Using symmetry in \(y\): \[I_1 = 2 \int_{0}^{1} \left( x^2 y + \frac{y^3}{3} \right)_{0}^{x} \, dx + 2 \int_{1}^{2} \left( x^2 y + \frac{y^3}{3} \right)_{0}^{(2-x)} \, dx\] \[I_1 = 2 \int_{0}^{1} \frac{4}{3} x^3 \, dx + 2 \int_{1}^{2} \left( x^2(2-x) + \frac{(2-x)^3}{3} \right) \, dx\] Evaluating the integrals: \[I_1 = \frac{8}{3} \left( \frac{1}{4} \right) + 2 \left[ \frac{2x^3}{3} - \frac{x^4}{4} + \frac{1}{3} \frac{(2-x)^4}{-4} \right]_{1}^{2}\] \[I_1 = \frac{8}{12} + 2 \left[ \left( \frac{16}{3} - 4 - \frac{1}{12}(0) \right) - \left( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{12} \right) \right]\] \[I_1 = \frac{2}{3} + 2 \left[ \frac{4}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \right] = \frac{2}{3} + 2 = \frac{8}{3}\] For \(I_2\): \[I_2 = \text{Area of square } R = \sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2} = 2\] Final Value: \[I = I_1 - I_2 = \frac{8}{3} - 2 = \frac{2}{3}\] \[\boxed{0.67}\]
Key points
  • The area of a region \(R\) is given by \(\iint\limits_{R} dxdy\).

questions.question: Consider the differential equation \(\dot{\vec{w}} = A\vec{w}\), with \[\vec{w}(t = 0) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\]. If \(\vec{w}(t) = e^{t}\vec{u}_x + e^{-2t}\vec{u}_y\) be the solution to the equation where \(\vec{u}_x\) and \(\vec{u}_y\) are unit vectors along the positive \(x\) and \(y\) axes respectively, then which of the following options is the correct matrix representing \(A\)?
questions.explanation: Given solution is \[\vec{w}(t) = e^t\vec{u}_x + e^{-2t}\vec{u}_y\] Since \(\vec{u}_x\) and \(\vec{u}_y\) are unit vectors along the positive \(x\) and \(y\) axes respectively, \[\vec{u}_x = \begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}\] and \[\vec{u}_y = \begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}\], \[\vec{w}(t) = e^t\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix} + e^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} e^t \\ e^{-2t} \end{bmatrix}\] The differential equation is \[\dot{\vec{w}} = A\vec{w}\] Solving LHS by differentiating \(\vec{w}(t)\) with respect to \(t\), \[\dot{\vec{w}}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} e^t \\ -2e^{-2t} \end{bmatrix}\] Let \[A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b\\ c & d \end{bmatrix}\] Then solving RHS, \[A\vec{w}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} a & b\\ c & d \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} e^t\\ e^{-2t} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} ae^t + be^{-2t}\\ ce^t + de^{-2t} \end{bmatrix}\] On comparing, we get \[ae^t + be^{-2t} = e^t\] \[ce^t + de^{-2t} = -2e^{-2t}\] Equating coefficients, \[a=1,\qquad b=0\] \[c=0,\qquad d=-2\] Hence, \[A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\] \[\boxed{\text{(A)}\ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}}\]

questions.question: Let \(X, N, Y\) and \(Z\) be random variables. The variables \(X\) and \(N\) are independent of each other. \(X\) is uniformly distributed between -1 and 1; \(N\) follows Normal distribution with zero mean and unity variance. \(Y\) and \(Z\) are defined as, \(Y\) = \(X + N\) and \(Z\) = \(X^2 + N\). Which of the following pairs represents the values of correlation between \(X\) and \(Y\) and that between \(X\) and \(Z\)?
questions.explanation: Since \(Y = X + N\) and \(Z = X^2 + N\),the covariance is evaluated using the independence of \(X\) and \(N\). Given: \[X \sim U(-1,1), \qquad N \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\] For a uniform random variable over \((-1,1)\), \[E[X] = 0, \qquad  E[X^2] = \frac{1}{3}, \qquad E[X^3] = 0\] Also, for the Gaussian random variable, \[E[N] = 0\] Correlation between \(X\) and \(Y\): \[\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y]\] \[\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) = E[X(X+N)] - 0 \qquad (\because Y = X + N)\] \[= E[X^2] + E[XN] = \frac{1}{3} + 0\] \[E[XN] = E[X]E[N] = 0 \qquad (\because X\ and\ N\ are\ independent)]\] \[\mathrm \Rightarrow\ {Cov}(X,Y) = \frac{1}{3}\] Correlation between \(X\) and \(Z\): \[\mathrm{Cov}(X,Z) = E[XZ] - E[X]E[Z]\] \[\mathrm{Cov}(X,Z) = E[X(X^2+N)] \qquad (\because Z = X^2 + N)\] \[= E[X^3] + E[XN] = 0 + 0\] \[\mathrm \Rightarrow\ {Cov}(X,Z) = 0\]

questions.question: The relation between the input current (\(I\)) and the output voltage (\(V\)) of a circuit is governed by; \[C\frac{dV}{dt}=I(t)-m(t).\] The circuit is excited by \(I(t)=q\delta(t),\) where \(q\) is a real-valued constant. The voltage at \(t=0^{-}\) is \(V_0\). Which of the following is an equivalent representation of the above case?
questions.explanation: Given, \[C\frac{dV}{dt}=I(t)-m(t), \quad \text{where; }\ I(t)=q\delta(t)\] The circuit equivalent to the above equation can be represented as; Substituting \(I(t)=q\delta(t)\), \[C\frac{dV}{dt}=q\delta(t)-m(t).\] Integrating both sides from \(0^-\) to \(0^+\), \[\int_{0^-}^{0^+}C\,dV = q\int_{0^-}^{0^+}\delta(t)\,dt - \int_{0^-}^{0^+}m(t)\,dt\] \[CV(0^+)-CV(0^-) = q - \int_{0^-}^{0^+}m(t)\,dt.\] Hence, \[V(0^+) = V_0+\frac{q}{C} - \frac{1}{C} \int_{0^-}^{0^+}m(t)\,dt \qquad\cdots(1)\] Now consider the equivalent representation, \[C\frac{dV}{dt}=-m(t)\] Integrating from \(0^-\) to \(0^+\), \[CV(0^+)-CV(0^-) = - \int_{0^-}^{0^+}m(t)\,dt\] \[V(0^+) = V(0^-) - \frac{1}{C} \int_{0^-}^{0^+}m(t)\,dt \qquad\cdots(2)\] Comparing equations (1) and (2), \[V(0^-) = V_0+\frac{q}{C}.\] Thus, the impulse current is absorbed into the initial capacitor voltage, and the equivalent equation becomes \[C\frac{dV}{dt}=-m(t), \qquad V(0^-)=V_0+\frac{q}{C}.\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{A. }C\frac{dV}{dt}=-m(t), \qquad V(0^-)=V_0+\frac{q}{C}}\]

questions.question: In the given circuit, \(L = 1~\mu\text{H}\) and \(C = 1~\mu\text{F}\). The phasor diagram for \(I_C\) and \(I_L\) is also shown. Assume that the phase \((\theta_1 + \theta_2)\) is \(90^\circ\) at a frequency of \(159.15~\text{kHz}\). Among the following options, what is the nearest integer value of \(R_C \times R_L\)?
questions.explanation: The currents \(I_C\) and \(I_L\) as shown in the figure are given by: \[I_{C} = \frac{V}{R_{C} + \frac{1}{j\omega C}} = \frac{V}{R_{C} - \frac{j}{\omega C}} = \frac{V}{\sqrt{R_{C}^{2} + \left(\frac{1}{\omega C}\right)^{2}}} \angle \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{\omega C R_{C}} \right)\] \[I_{L} = \frac{V}{R_{L} + j\omega L} = \frac{V}{\sqrt{R_{L}^{2} + (\omega L)^{2}}} \angle -\tan^{-1} \left( \frac{\omega L}{R_{L}} \right)\] The phase angles \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) can be defined as: \[\theta_{1} = \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{\omega C R_{C}} \right)\] \[\theta_{2} = \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{\omega L}{R_{L}} \right)\] Given the condition that the sum of the phase angles is \(90^\circ\): \[\theta_{1} + \theta_{2} = 90^\circ\] Taking the tangent of both sides: \[\tan(\theta_{1} + \theta_{2}) = \tan 90^\circ\] Using the trigonometric identity \(\tan(A+B) = \frac{\tan A + \tan B}{1 - \tan A \tan B}\), the expression becomes infinite when the denominator is zero: \[\frac{\frac{1}{\omega C R_{C}} + \frac{\omega L}{R_{L}}}{1 - \left( \frac{1}{\omega C R_{C}} \cdot \frac{\omega L}{R_{L}} \right)} \to \infty\] Equating the denominator to zero: \[1 - \frac{1}{R_{C} R_{L}} \cdot \frac{\omega L}{\omega C} = 0\] \[1 = \frac{1}{R_{C} R_{L}} \cdot \frac{L}{C}\] \[R_{C} R_{L} = \frac{L}{C}\] For the specific circuit parameters provided in the derivation: \[\boxed{R_{C} R_{L} = 1}\] Since the frequency is fixed at \(159.15\,\text{kHz}\), we do not explore any other solutions by further simplifying the expressions. \[\boxed{(b) 1}\]

questions.question: Consider the two-port network as shown in the Figure. Which of the following options provides the correct set of values of A, B, C and D parameters?
questions.explanation:
We need to find out the ABCD parameters of the corresponding network. This can be done using the following approaches.
Method 1
Calculating ABCD parameters from mesh equations:
Applying Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) in the respective loops of the two-port network: KVL in mesh 1: \[V_{1} = 2\text{k} I_{1} + 1\text{k} I_{2} \quad \text{--- (1)}\] KVL in mesh 2: \[V_{2} = 2\text{k} I_{2} + 1\text{k} I_{1} \quad \text{--- (2)}\] The general form of the ABCD parameters is defined as: \[V_{1} = A V_{2} - B I_{2} \quad \text{--- (3)}\] \[I_{1} = C V_{2} - D I_{2} \quad \text{--- (4)}\] From equation (2), we can express \(I_{1}\) in terms of \(V_{2}\) and \(I_{2}\): \[1\text{k} I_{1} = V_{2} - 2\text{k} I_{2}\] \[I_{1} = \frac{1}{10^{3}} V_{2} - \frac{2\times 10^{3}}{10^{3}} I_{2}\] \[I_{1} = 10^{-3} V_{2} - 2 I_{2} \quad \text{--- (5)}\] Comparing equation (5) with the standard form in equation (4): \[\therefore C = 10^{-3}, \quad D = 2\] Substituting equation (5) into equation (1): \[V_{1} = 2\text{k} (10^{-3} V_{2} - 2 I_{2}) + 1\text{k} I_{2}\] \[V_{1} = (2 \times 10^{3} \times 10^{-3}) V_{2} - (4\times 10^{3}) I_{2} + 1\text{k} I_{2}\] \[V_{1} = 2 V_{2} - 3\text{k} I_{2} \quad \text{--- (6)}\] Comparing equation (6) with the standard form in equation (3): \[\therefore A = 2, \quad B = 3 \times 10^{3}\]
Method 2
Calculating ABCD parameters by opening and shorting of respective ports:
The general form of ABCD parameters is: \[V_{1} = A V_{2} - B I_{2} \quad \text{--- (1)}\] \[I_{1} = C V_{2} - D I_{2} \quad \text{--- (2)}\] The parameters are defined under specific port conditions: \[A = \left. \frac{V_{1}}{V_{2}} \right|_{I_{2}=0}, \quad B = \left. -\frac{V_{1}}{I_{2}} \right|_{V_{2}=0}, \quad C = \left. \frac{I_{1}}{V_{2}} \right|_{I_{2}=0}, \quad D = \left. -\frac{I_{1}}{I_{2}} \right|_{V_{2}=0}\] We analyze the circuit for two conditions:
  • Keeping Port 2 open (\(I_2=0\))
  • Keeping Port 2 shorted (\(V_2=0\))
1. Port 2 Open (\(I_{2} = 0\)):
\[V_{2} = I_{1} (1\,\text{k})\] \[I_{1} = \frac{V_{1}}{1\,\text{k} + 1\,\text{k}} = \frac{V_{1}}{2\,\text{k}}\] Substituting \(I_{1}\) in the \(V_{2}\) equation: \[V_{2} = \frac{V_{1}}{2\,\text{k}} (1\,\text{k}) = \frac{V_{1}}{2} \implies A = \left. \frac{V_{1}}{V_{2}} \right|_{I_{2}=0}=2\] \[C = \left. \frac{I_{1}}{V_{2}} \right|_{I_{2}=0} = \frac{1}{1\,\text{k}} = 10^{-3}\] 2. Port 2 Shorted (\(V_{2} = 0\)):
When port 2 is shorted, the shunt \(1\,\text{k}\Omega\) resistor is in parallel with the output \(1\,\text{k}\Omega\) resistor. The total resistance seen at port 1 is: \[R_{in} = 1\,\text{k} + (1\,\text{k} \parallel 1\,\text{k}) = 1\,\text{k} + 0.5\,\text{k} = 1.5\,\text{k}\Omega\] \[V_{1} = I_{1} (1.5\,\text{k})\] By current division, the output current \(I_{2}\) (defined entering the port) is: \[I_{2} = - \frac{I_{1}}{2} \implies D = \left. -\frac{I_{1}}{I_{2}} \right|_{V_{2}=0} = 2\] Substituting \(I_{1} = -2 I_{2}\) into the \(V_{1}\) equation: \[V_{1} = -2 I_{2} (1.5\,\text{k}) = -3\,\text{k} I_{2}\] \[B = \left. -\frac{V_{1}}{I_{2}} \right|_{V_{2}=0} = 3\,\text{k}\]
Method 3
Transforming Z parameters to ABCD parameters:
The given Z parameters for the network are: \[Z = \begin{bmatrix} 2\times 10^{3} & 1\times 10^{3} \\ 1\times 10^{3} & 2\times 10^{3} \end{bmatrix}\] From the Z-parameter definition, we have: \[V_{1} = 2\times 10^{3} I_{1} + 10^{3} I_{2} \quad \text{--- (1)}\] \[V_{2} = 10^{3} I_{1} + 2\times 10^{3} I_{2} \quad \text{--- (2)}\] From equation (2), we can express \(I_{1}\) in terms of \(V_{2}\) and \(I_{2}\): \[10^{3} I_{1} = V_{2} - 2\times 10^{3} I_{2}\] \[I_{1} = \frac{1}{10^{3}} V_{2} - \frac{2\times 10^{3}}{10^{3}} I_{2}\] \[I_{1} = 10^{-3} V_{2} - 2 I_{2} \quad \text{--- (3)}\] Comparing this with the ABCD parameter equation \(I_{1} = C V_{2} - D I_{2}\), we get: \[C = 10^{-3}\,\Omega^{-1}\] \[D = 2\] Substituting \(I_{1}\) from equation (3) into equation (1): \[V_{1} = 2\times 10^{3} (10^{-3} V_{2} - 2 I_{2}) + 10^{3} I_{2}\] \[V_{1} = (2\times 10^{3} \times 10^{-3}) V_{2} - (2\times 10^{3} \times 2) I_{2} + 10^{3} I_{2}\] \[V_{1} = 2 V_{2} - 4\times 10^{3} I_{2} + 10^{3} I_{2}\] \[V_{1} = 2 V_{2} - 3\times 10^{3} I_{2} \quad \text{--- (4)}\] Comparing this with the ABCD parameter equation \(V_{1} = A V_{2} - B I_{2}\), we get: \[\therefore A = 2\] \[B = 3\times 10^{3}\,\Omega\]
Key points
  • Unit Check: \(A\) and \(D\) are dimensionless, \(B\) has units of Ohms (\(\Omega\)), and \(C\) has units of Siemens (S).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Sign Convention : Ensure you take the direction of the port currents and their corresponding signs in the ABCD parameter equation correctly. For example, if port-2 current enters the network, we will have the equations used in the solution above. However, if the current leaves the network, the '-' signs will be replaced by '+' signs (as in transmission lines).
\[\boxed{(d) A=2, B = 3 \times 10^3\,\Omega, C = 10^{-3}\,\Omega^{-1},D =2}\]

questions.question: Consider a real signal \(x(t)\), \(-\infty<t<\infty\), such that \(x(t)=0\) for \(t<0\), \(x(t)=2\) for \(0\leq t<1\) and \(x(t)=0\) for \(t\geq 1\). Let \(E[x(t)]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}[x(t)]^2\,dt\). Which of the following options correctly represents the ratio, \(E[x(t)]/E[3\,x(-3t+5)]\)?
questions.explanation:
Let \[E[x(t)]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|^2\,dt.\] Since \[x(t)=
\begin{cases}
2, & 0\le t<1,\\
0, & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}\] its energy is \[E[x(t)]
=\int_{0}^{1}2^2\,dt
=4.\] For \[y(t)=3x(-3t+5),\] the scaling property of energy gives \[E[Ax(at+b)]
=\frac{|A|^2}{|a|}E[x(t)].\] Here, \[A=3,\qquad a=-3.\] Hence, \[E[3x(-3t+5)]
=\frac{3^2}{3}E[x(t)]
=3E[x(t)]
=12.\] Therefore, \[\frac{E[x(t)]}{E[3x(-3t+5)]}
=\frac{4}{12}
=\frac{1}{3}.\] \[\boxed{\text{(c)} \dfrac{1}{3}}\]

questions.question: The continuous time signal \(x(t)\) is real, periodic with period \(T\) and satisfies the Dirichlet conditions. The Fourier series representation of \[x(t) = \sum_{-\infty}^{\infty} a_n e^{j\left(\frac{2\pi nt}{T}\right)}\] and \(x(t)\) satisfies the following: \(x\left(t - \frac{T}{2}\right) = -x(t)\). For any integer \(m\), which of the following options is correct?
questions.explanation:
Given that, \[x\left(t - \frac{T}{2}\right) = -x(t)\] where '\(T\)' is FTP. Thus, \(x(t)\) is half-wave symmetric signal. For HWS: Even harmonics will be absent i.e. \(a_n = 0\) if \(n\) is even-integer. \[\Rightarrow a_{2m} = 0 \text{ where } m = \text{integer}\] \[\boxed{{A) a_{2m} = 0}}\]
Key points
  • A periodic signal \(x(t)\) with a fundamental time period \(T\) possesses Half-Wave Symmetry (HWS) if it satisfies the condition \(x(t \pm T/2) = -x(t)\).
  • A key property of half-wave symmetric signals is that their Fourier series expansion contains only odd harmonics. All even harmonics evaluate to zero (\(a_n = 0\) for all even integers \(n\)).

questions.question: Two analog signals \(x_1(t)\) and \(x_2(t)\) (\(t\) in second), are sampled at a rate \(F_s = 40\,\text{Hz}\), where \(x_1(t) = \cos(20\pi t), t \geq 0\) and \(x_2(t) = \cos(100\pi t), t \geq 0\). The first ten samples (starting from \(t = 0\)) are considered for the analysis. Which of the following statements is TRUE?
options: All of the first three samples of \(x_1(t)\) are greater than the corresponding samples of \(x_2(t)\).
All of the last three samples of \(x_1(t)\) are greater than the corresponding samples of \(x_2(t)\).
All of the samples of \(x_2(t)\) are greater than the corresponding samples of \(x_1(t)\).
All of the fourth to seventh samples of \(x_1(t)\) are equal to the corresponding samples of \(x_2(t)\).
questions.explanation:
\(x_1(t) = \cos 20\pi t\) On sampling \[t = nT_s = \frac{n}{f_s} = \frac{n}{40}\] \[x_1(n) = x_1(nT_s) = \cos\left( 20\pi \times \frac{n}{40} \right) = \cos \frac{\pi}{2} n\] Similarly, for \(x_2(t)\) \[x_2(t) = \cos 100\pi t\] On sampling \[t = nT_s = \frac{n}{40}\] \[x_2(n) = x_2(nT_s) = \cos\left( 100\pi \frac{n}{40} \right) = \cos\left( \frac{5\pi}{2} n \right)\] \[= \cos\left[ \left( 2\pi + \frac{\pi}{2} \right) n \right] = \cos \frac{\pi}{2} n\] Therefore, \[x_1(n) = x_2(n)\] Hence, all of the fourth to seventh samples of \(x_1(t)\) are equal to the corresponding samples of \(x_2(t)\). \[\boxed{\text{D) All of the fourth to seventh samples of $x_1(t)$ are equal to the corresponding samples of $x_2(t)$. }}\]
Key points
  • Aliasing Concept: When sampling a continuous-time signal, frequency components that differ by integer multiples of the sampling frequency (\(f_s\)) map to the same discrete-time sequence.
  • Discrete Cosine Periodicity: The sequence \(\cos(\omega_0 n)\) is periodic with respect to the digital frequency \(\omega_0\) with period \(2\pi\). That is, \(\cos((\omega_0 + 2\pi m)n) = \cos(\omega_0 n)\) for any integer \(m\).

questions.question: The response of a discrete time system \(y[n]\) obeys the following relation: \(y[n] = \frac{5}{6}y[n - 1] - \frac{1}{6}y[n - 2] + x[n]\). The input to the system is \(x[n] = \delta[n] - \frac{1}{3}\delta[n - 1]\). Which of the following options is TRUE for \(y[n]\) ?
questions.explanation:
The given difference equation is: \[y(n) = \frac{5}{6}y(n - 1) - \frac{1}{6}y(n - 2) + x(n)\] Taking the \(z\)-transform on both sides: \[Y(z) = \frac{5}{6}z^{-1}Y(z) - \frac{1}{6}z^{-2}Y(z) + X(z)\] \[Y(z)\left(1 - \frac{5}{6}z^{-1} + \frac{1}{6}z^{-2}\right) = X(z)\] \[H(z) = \frac{Y(z)}{X(z)} = \frac{1}{1 - \frac{5}{6}z^{-1} + \frac{1}{6}z^{-2}}\] On factoring the denominator, we get, \[H(z) = \frac{1}{\left(1 - \frac{1}{2}z^{-1}\right)\left(1 - \frac{1}{3}z^{-1}\right)}\] The input is given as \[x[n] = \delta[n] - \frac{1}{3}\delta[n - 1]\] Its \(z\)-transform is: \[X(z) = 1 - \frac{1}{3}z^{-1}\] The response \(Y(z)\), \[Y(z) = H(z) \cdot X(z)\] \[Y(z) = \frac{1 - \frac{1}{3}z^{-1}}{\left(1 - \frac{1}{2}z^{-1}\right) \left(1 - \frac{1}{3}z^{-1}\right)}\] \[Y(z) = \frac{1}{1 - \frac{1}{2}z^{-1}}\] On taking inverse \(z\)-transform of \(Y(z)\), we get \[y(n) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n u(n)\] Since \(y(n) = 0\) for \(n < 0\). Hence, the response is causal. The pole of \(Y(z)\) is at \(z = \frac{1}{2}\). Since the magnitude of the pole (i.e. \(\frac{1}{2}\)) i.e. less than \(1\) , the pole lies inside the unit circle in the \(z\)-plane, making the response stable. Hence, the response \(y[n]\) is stable and causal. \[\boxed{\text{A. Stable and causal response}}\]
Key points
  • The \(z\)-transform of a time-shifted signal \(x[n-k]\) is \(z^{-k}X(z)\).
  • A discrete-time LTI system is stable if all poles of its transfer function lie strictly inside the unit circle (\(|z| < 1\)).
  • A system (or response) is causal if its time-domain sequence is zero for \(n < 0\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not evaluate stability based solely on the poles of the system transfer function \(H(z)\) if the question asks for the stability of the response \(Y(z)\). Always perform pole-zero cancellations between \(H(z)\) and \(X(z)\) first.

questions.question: Consider that the concentration of electrons in a semiconductor bar varies linearly from \(2 \times 10^{17}\text{ cm}^{-3}\) at \(x = 1\text{ }\mu\text{m}\) to \(1 \times 10^{16}\text{ cm}^{-3}\) at \(x = 4\text{ }\mu\text{m}\) along the \(x\)-direction. Assume that the concentration of electrons is not varying along other directions (that is along \(y\)- and \(z\)-directions). [Given: the mobility of electron is \(1400\text{ cm}^2\text{V}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}\), thermal voltage is \(25\text{ mV}\) and electronic charge is \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\).] The density of electron diffusion current (in \(\text{A/mm}^2\)) is ___. (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] The diffusion constant \(D_{n}\) is calculated using Einstein's relation: \[D_{n} = \mu_{n} V_{T} = 1400 \times 25 \times 10^{-3} = 35\,\text{cm}^{2}/\text{s}\] The electron concentration \(n(x)\) varies linearly from \(x = 1\,\mu\text{m}\) to \(x = 4\,\mu\text{m}\). The concentration gradient is: \[\frac{dn(x)}{dx} = \frac{n(4\,\mu\text{m}) - n(1\,\mu\text{m})}{4\,\mu \text{m} - 1\,\mu\text{m}}\] \[\frac{dn(x)}{dx} = \frac{10^{16} - 2 \times 10^{17}}{3 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{cm}} = \frac{-1.9 \times 10^{17}}{3 \times 10^{-4}} \approx -6.33 \times 10^{20}\,\text{cm}^{-4}\] Now, it is observed that electron concentration decreases along positive-X axis, which implies the diffusion current flows along the negative-X axis direction. Here, since the direction of diffusion current has not been specified, both positive and negative values are correct. The diffusion current density \(J_{\text{diff}}\) is given by: \[J_{\text{diff}} = q D_{n} \frac{dn(x)}{dx}\] Taking the magnitude: \[|J_{\text{diff}}| = \left| 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 35 \times (-6.33 \times 10^{20}) \right|\] \[|J_{\text{diff}}| = 3544.8 \, \text{A}/\text{cm}^{2} \approx 35.45\,\text{A}/\text{mm}^{2}\] As the direction of current is not specified, the answer is: \[\boxed{35.45\text{ OR }-35.45}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Ensure consistent units; convert the distance \(x\) from \(\mu\text{m}\) to \(\text{cm}\) (\(1\,\mu\text{m} = 10^{-4}\,\text{cm}\)) before calculating the gradient.
  • Do not confuse the sign convention; electron diffusion current flows opposite to the direction of electron diffusion.

questions.question: Consider carrier transport in a Zener diode in the breakdown region. Which is the dominant transport mechanism for current flow in this case?
questions.explanation:
In a heavily doped \(p\)-\(n\) junction, the depletion region width is extremely narrow. When a reverse bias is applied, the high electric field generated across this thin layer allows electrons to move from the valence band of the \(p\)-side to the conduction band of the \(n\)-side through a process known as quantum mechanical tunneling. This phenomenon is characteristic of Zener breakdown. \[\boxed{(C) \text{Tunneling}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse Zener breakdown with Avalanche breakdown, which is caused by impact ionization in lightly doped junctions.

questions.question: Consider a p-n junction diode when it is forward biased with \(2 \text{ V}\). Which of the following is/are the correct magnitude(s) of the energy difference between quasi Fermi-levels, \(E_{fn}\) in the n-side and \(E_{fp}\) in the p-side?
questions.explanation:
In a forward-biased \(p\)-\(n\) junction, the carrier concentrations depart from their equilibrium values, necessitating the use of quasi-Fermi levels \(E_{FN}\) and \(E_{FP}\) to describe the electron and hole distributions respectively. The separation between these two levels is directly proportional to the applied forward bias voltage \(V\). The relationship between the quasi-Fermi level separation and the applied voltage is given by: \[E_{FN} - E_{FP} = qV\] Given an applied forward bias voltage \(V = 2\,\text{V}\), the magnitude of the difference between the quasi-Fermi levels is: \[|E_{FN} - E_{FP}| = q(2\,\text{V}) = 2\,\text{eV}\] \[\boxed{(A)\, 2 \text{ eV}}\]
Key points
  • Quasi-Fermi Levels: Used to describe the population of electrons and holes when a semiconductor is not in thermal equilibrium (e.g., under bias or illumination).
  • Bias Relationship: The separation \(E_{FN} - E_{FP}\) at any point in the depletion region is equal to the energy equivalent of the applied potential \(qV\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse the separation of quasi-Fermi levels with the built-in potential \(V_{bi}\).

questions.question: An \(n\)-channel MOSFET is connected as shown in the Figure. Assume \(V_{TH} = 1\,\text{V}\), \(V_{DD} = 5\,\text{V}\), and \(\mu C_{ox} \left(\dfrac{W}{L}\right) = 2\,\text{mA}\,\text{V}^{-2}\) and neglect channel length modulation effects. The gate voltage (\(V_G\)) of the \(n\)-channel MOSFET (in Volt) is ________. (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation:
Given circuit is, To find the gate voltage \(V_G\) of the n-channel MOSFET, we start by analyzing the circuit. The MOSFET is in saturation since it's connected as a source follower with \(V_{DD} > V_{TH}\). The current equation in saturation is: \[I_{DS} = \frac{1}{2}\mu C_{ox} \left(\frac{W}{L}\right) (V_{GS} - V_{TH})^2\] Here, the drain current (\(I_D\)) through the \(1\,\text{k}\Omega\) resistor can be calculated as: \[I_D = \frac{V_{DD} - V_G}{1\,\text{k}\Omega}\] Equating both expressions for \(I_D\): \[\frac{V_{DD} - V_G}{1\,\text{k}\Omega} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2\,\text{mA/V}^2 \cdot (V_G - V_{TH})^2\] \[V_{DD} - V_G = (V_G - V_{TH})^2\] Substitute \(V_{DD} = 5\,\text{V}\) and \(V_{TH} = 1\,\text{V}\): \[5 - V_G = (V_G - 1)^2\] \[5 - V_G = V_G^2 - 2V_G + 1\] \[V_G^2 - V_G - 4 = 0\] Using the quadratic formula \(V_G = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\), where \(a = 1, b = -1, c = -4\): \[V_G = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 16}}{2}\] \[V_G = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2}\] \[V_G = \frac{1 \pm 4.12}{2}\] Calculating the positive root (ensures \(V_{GS} > V_{TH}\)): \[\boxed{V_G = \frac{5.12}{2} = 2.56\,\text{V}}\]
Key points
  • When the gate of an N-MOSFET is tied to its drain then it is always in saturation as \(V_{DS}\) is always grater than \(V_{GS} - V_{TH} = V_{DS} - V_{TH}\) .
  • Always select the positive root of the quadratic equation that satisfies the strong inversion condition \(V_{GS} > V_{TH}\).

questions.question: The ideal OP-AMP circuit shown in the Figure produces output voltage \(V_o = x\) when the Switch, S, is open. Which of the options represents the output voltage when S is closed?
questions.explanation:
The circuit after closing the switch is, Given, \(V_{o1} = x\) (before closing the switch) When the switch is open, the feedback resistance is the sum of both resistors in the feedback path (\(2\,\text{k}\Omega + 1\,\text{k}\Omega = 3\,\text{k}\Omega\)). \[\text{Switch open} \implies V_{o1} = \left(1 + \frac{R_f}{R_1}\right) V_i=\left(1 + \frac{3}{1}\right) \times 1 = 4\,\text{V} = x\] When the switch is closed, the \(1\,\text{k}\Omega\) resistor is shorted out, leaving only the \(2\,\text{k}\Omega\) resistor as the effective feedback resistance. \[\text{Switch closed} \implies V_{o2} = \left(1 + \frac{2}{1}\right) \times 1 = 3\,\text{V}\] Now, taking the ratio of the output voltages: \[\frac{V_{o2}}{V_{o1}} = \frac{3}{4} \implies V_{o2} = \frac{3}{4}x\] \[\boxed{\text{(C)\quad}\frac{3}{4}x}\]
Key points
  • The output voltage of a standard non-inverting Op-Amp in negative feedback is given by \(V_o = \left(1 + \frac{R_f}{R_1}\right)V_i\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Always check which type of feedback is present.

questions.question: A circuit using an ideal OP-AMP is shown in the Figure. Which of the following options gives the correct value of the current \(I_x\)?
questions.explanation:
Given circuit is, Since the op-amp is connected in negative feedback and it is an inverting amplifier(since input is connected at inverting terminal), \[V_0 = \frac{-R_f}{R_1}V_i =\frac{-1}{1} \times 2 = -2\,\text{V}\] Applying KCL at \(V_0\), \[I_x = I_1 + I_2\] \[I_x = \frac{0 - V_0}{1} + \frac{0 - V_0}{2}\] \[I_x = \frac{2}{1} + \frac{2}{2} = 3\,\text{mA}\] \[\boxed{\text{(C)\quad 3.0 mA}}\]
Key points
  • Virtual Ground: In an ideal op-amp with the non-inverting terminal grounded, the voltage at the inverting terminal is forced to \(0\,\text{V}\).
  • Inverting Amplifier Gain: The output voltage \(V_0\) at the feedback node is determined by the ratio of the feedback resistor to the input resistor: \(V_0 = -\left(\frac{R_f}{R_{in}}\right) V_{in}\).

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: Consider an ideal OP-AMP circuit as shown in the Figure. The resistances \(R_1 = R_2 = R_3 = R_4 = 50\text{ k}\Omega\). The magnitude of the closed loop gain is _______. (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Given circuit is, Here, the feeback network is a T-network and its effective resistance is given by, \[R_f = R_2 + R_3 + \frac{R_2 R_3}{R_4}\] \[\therefore \text{Closed loop gain }\frac{V_0}{V_i} = \frac{-R_f}{R_1}=\frac{ -(R_2 + R_3 + \frac{R_2 R_3}{R_4})}{R_1}\] \[\frac{V_0}{V_i} = \frac{-R_2}{R_1} \left[ 1 + \frac{R_3}{R_2} + \frac{R_3}{R_4} \right]\] \[= \frac{-50\,\text{k}\Omega}{50\,\text{k}\Omega} \left[ 1 + \frac{50\,\text{k}\Omega}{50\,\text{k}\Omega} + \frac{50\,\text{k}\Omega}{50\,\text{k}\Omega} \right]\] \[= -1[1 + 1 + 1] = -3\] Hence, \[{\left| \frac{V_0}{V_i} \right| = 3}\]
Method 2
The circuit is, Because of virtual ground due to negative feedback and ideal op-amp, \(V_+ = V_- = 0\,\text{V}\) Since no current flows into input terminals of Op-Amp, entire I flows into \(R_2\) and is given by, \[I = \frac{V_i - 0}{50\,\text{k}}=\frac{V_i}{50k}\] \[V = 0 - R_2 I = -50\,\text{k} \left(\frac{V_i}{50\,\text{k}}\right) = -V_i\] Apply KCL at \(V\), \[\frac{V - 0}{50} + \frac{V}{50} + \frac{V - V_o}{50} = 0\] \[V + V + V - V_o = 0\] \[3V - V_o = 0\] \[V_o = 3V \implies V_o = 3(-V_{i})\] \[\frac{V_o}{V_{i}}=-3\] \[\boxed{\left|\frac{V_o}{V_{i}}\right|=3}\]
Key points
  • The equivalent feedback resistance of the T-network formed by \(R_2\), \(R_3\), and \(R_4\) is \(R_{eq} = R_2 + R_3 + \frac{R_2 R_3}{R_4}\).

questions.question: Consider the circuit shown in the Figure with \(V_i = 3\text{ V}\) and \(V_{CC} = 12\text{ V}\). Assume \(V_{BE} = 0.7\text{ V}\) and \(\beta_{dc} = 99\) for the BJT. Which of the following options is the correct value of the current \(I_o\)?
questions.explanation:
From the virtual short concept of the ideal op-amp, \[V^- = V^+ = 3\,\text{V}\] The voltage at the emitter of the BJT is connected to the inverting terminal, so the emitter voltage \(V_E = 3\,\text{V}\). The emitter current \(I_E\) can be calculated as: \[I_E = \frac{V_E}{1\,\text{k}\Omega} = \frac{3}{1\,\text{k}\Omega} = 3\,\text{mA}\] The output current of the op-amp \(I_0\) flows directly into the base of the BJT, meaning \(I_0 = I_B\). Using the standard BJT current relationship for the active region: \[I_0 = I_B = \frac{I_E}{1 + \beta}\] \[I_0 = \frac{3\,\text{mA}}{1 + 99} = \frac{3}{100}\,\text{mA} = 0.03\,\text{mA}\] \[I_0 = 30\,\mu\text{A}\] \[\boxed{\text{(D)\quad 30 }\mu\text{A}}\]
Key points
  • BJT Current Relationship: In the active region, the relationship between the emitter current and base current is defined by \(I_E = (1 + \beta)I_B\). The op-amp only needs to supply the required base current.

questions.question: A small signal source, \(V_i(t) = A \cos(10^5 t) + B \sin(10^7 t)\) is applied to a BJT circuit as shown in the Figure. Assume zero source resistance, \(V_{BE} = 0.7\text{ V}\), \(\beta_{dc} = 99\), Early voltage \(= 100\text{ V}\) and Thermal voltage \(= 25\text{ mV}\). Effect of internal parasitic capacitances of the BJT may be neglected. Which expression is the best approximation of the output voltage \(V_o(t)\)?
questions.explanation:
Given early voltage (\(V_A\)) = 100 V, Thermal voltage (\(V_T\)) = 25 mV, \(V_{BE}\)=0.7 V and \(\beta = 99\). and \(V_i = A\cos{(10^5t)}+B\sin{(10^7t)}\) Given circuit is, Case-1 : DC Analysis For DC analysis, open circuit the capacitors and deactivate AC sources. Replacing the bias network with its Thevenin's equivalent, where \[V_{th} = \frac{12 \times 25}{100 + 25} = 2.4\,\text{V}\] \[R_{th} = 100 \parallel 25 = 20\,\text{k}\Omega\] The equivalent circuit is given by, Applying KVL in base emitter loop, \[V_{th}-I_BR_{th}-V_{BE}-I_ER_E=0\] \[V_{th}-I_BR_{th}-V_{BE}-(1+\beta)I_BR_E=0\] \[I_B = \frac{V_{th} - V_{BE}}{R_{th} + (1 + \beta)R_E}\] \[I_B = 0.01\,\text{mA}\] \[I_C = \beta I_B = 0.99\,\text{mA}\] \[V_{CE} \cong V_{CC} - I_C(R_C + R_E) = 5.56\,\text{V}\] \[g_m = \frac{I_C}{V_T} = 39.6\,\text{m}\mho\] \[r_\pi = \frac{\beta}{g_m} = 2.5\,\text{k}\Omega\] \[r_o = \frac{V_A + V_{CE}}{I_C} = 106.6\,\text{k}\Omega\] Case-2 : AC Analysis Since the given input frequencies are very high, the capacitors offer very low impedance, so they can be short circuited. And \(r_0\) is very high compared to other resistances so it can be neglected. Hence for AC analysis, deactivate DC sources, short circuit capacitors, neglect \(r_0\) and replace bjt with \(\pi\)-model, the circuit becomes, \[V_0 = -g_mR_cV_{\pi}\] \[V_i = V_{\pi}+g_mV_{\pi}R_E= (1+g_mR_E)V_\pi\] \[A_v =\frac{V_0}{V_i}\cong \frac{-g_m R_C}{1 + g_m R_{E}}, \quad R_{E} = 0.5\,\text{k}\Omega\] \[A_v \cong -9.5\] \(100\,\text{nF}\) capacitors provide negligible reactance at given input frequencies. Hence both frequencies will appear in the output. \[V_o = A_v \times V_i\] \[V_o \cong -9.1 [A \cos (10^5 t) + B \sin (10^7 t)]\] \[\boxed{\text{(A)\quad}-9.1 [A \cos (10^5 t) + B \sin (10^7 t)]}\]
Key points
  • Small Signal Parameters: The BJT AC parameters depend on the DC operating point: \(g_m = I_C / V_T\), \(r_\pi = \beta / g_m\), and \(r_o = (V_A + V_{CE}) / I_C\).
  • Coupling Capacitors: At high frequencies (like \(10^5\) and \(10^7\,\text{rad/s}\)), the reactance of \(100\,\text{nF}\) coupling capacitors (\(X_C = 1/\omega C\)) is nearly zero, meaning they act as short circuits to the AC signal without attenuating it.

Method 1
Based on the provided K-map representation, we can identify two valid minimal sum-of-products (SOP) expressions depending on the chosen pairings: Pairing 1:
\[f = \bar{x}\bar{z} + xz + wy\bar{z}\] Pairing 2:

To verify other options, let's check the common term \(\bar{w}xy\bar{z}\) present in options (B) and (C). In binary, \(\bar{w}xy\bar{z}\) corresponds to \((0110)_2\), which is decimal \(6\). Locating it on the kmap- By inspecting the K-map, cell \(6\) is not a required minterm . Thus, any expression containing this term is incorrect. questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: What is the 10's complement of \((47)_{10}\)?
questions.explanation:
The problem asks for the \(10\)'s complement of the decimal value \((47)_{10}\). This can be determined by first finding the \((r-1)\)'s complement and then adding \(1\). Step 1: Find the \(9\)'s complement
Subtract each digit of the number from \(9\): \[\begin{array}{r@{\quad}l} 99 & \\ -\, 47 & \\ \hline 52 & \text{i.e., } (9\text{'s complement}) \end{array}\] Step 2: Find the \(10\)'s complement
Add \(1\) to the resulting \(9\)'s complement: \[\begin{array}{r@{\quad}l} 52 & \\ +\, 1 & \\ \hline 53 & \end{array}\] Thus, the \(10\)'s complement of \((47)_{10}\) is \(53\). \[\boxed{(B)53}\]
Key points
  • For a base \(r\) system, the \(r\)'s complement is defined as: \[r\text{'s complement} = (r-1)\text{'s complement} + 1\]
  • For decimal (\(r=10\)), the \(10\)'s complement is \((9\text{'s complement} + 1)\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not forget to add the \(1\) after finding the \((r-1)\)'s complement to reach the \(r\)'s complement.

questions.explanation:
Given: A negative edge-triggered JK flip-flop with \(J = K = 1\). When \(J = K = 1\), the JK-FF operates in toggle mode. The frequency of output \(Q\) is: \[f_{out} = \frac{f_{in}}{2}\] \[f_{out} = \frac{10}{2} = 5\,\text{Hz}\] \[\boxed{5}\]
Key points
  • \(J=K=1 \implies\) Toggle mode.
  • Output frequency \(f_{out} = f_{clk}/2\).

questions.question: A binary ripple counter is designed to count \((0)_{10}\) to \((64)_{10}\). Which of the following is/are the number of flip-flops required to design the counter?
questions.explanation:
To count from \(0\) to \(64\), the number of distinct states required is \(N = 64 - 0 + 1 = 65\) states. The number of flip-flops (\(n\)) must satisfy: \[2^n \geq N\] \[2^n \geq 65\] Checking values:
  • If \(n = 6\), \(2^6 = 64\) (Insufficient).
  • If \(n = 7\), \(2^7 = 128\) (Sufficient).
Therefore, 7 flip-flops are required. Hence, the correct option is (B). \[\boxed{(B)7}\]
Key points
  • \(n\)-bit counter max count \(= 2^n - 1\).

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: The address of the first location of a 256 kilo byte (KB) memory is \((2500)_{\text{H}}\). Choose the correct address of the last location of the memory.
questions.explanation:
Given:
  • Memory Size = \(256\,\text{KB}\)
  • First Location Address (Starting Address) = \((2500)_{H}\)
Step 1: Determine the total number of locations in the memory. Since the memory size is \(256\,\text{KB}\) and memory is typically byte-addressable: \[\text{Total Locations} = 256 \times 1024 = 262,144\,\text{locations}\] Step 2: Convert the total number of locations into hexadecimal to find the address range. \[256\,\text{K} = 2^{8} \times 2^{10} = 2^{18}\] In hexadecimal, \(2^{18}\) is calculated as: \[2^{18} = 2^{2} \times 2^{16} = 4 \times (16)^{4} = (40000)_{H}\] The total number of addresses (offset) starting from \(0\) would be from \((00000)_{H}\) to \((2^{18} - 1)_{H}\). \[\text{Offset} = (40000)_{H} - (1)_{H} = (3FFFF)_{H}\] Step 3: Calculate the Last Location Address. The last address is found by adding the offset to the starting address: \[\text{Last Address} = \text{Starting Address} + \text{Offset}\] \[\text{Last Address} = (02500)_{H} + (3FFFF)_{H}\] Performing the hexadecimal addition:
\(3\)\(F\)\(F\)\(F\)\(F\)
\(+\)\(0\)\(2\)\(5\)\(0\)\(0\)
\(4\)\(2\)\(4\)\(F\)\(F\)
The last location address is \((424FF)_{H}\). \[\boxed{(C)(424\text{FF})_{\text{H}}}\]
Key points
  • Memory Range: For a memory of size \(N\), the addresses range from \(S\) to \(S + (N - 1)\), where \(S\) is the starting address.
  • Hexadecimal Conversion: \(1\,\text{K} = 2^{10} = (400)_{H}\). Therefore, \(256\,\text{K} = 256 \times 2^{10} = (100)_{H} \times (400)_{H} = (40000)_{H}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Off-by-one error: Always remember to add \((N-1)\) to the starting address, not \(N\). Adding \(N\) gives the address of the location immediately following the memory block.
  • Hex Addition: Ensure carries are handled correctly in base-16 (\(F + 5 = 14\) in decimal, which is \(1\) carry and \(4\) in hex).

questions.ref: Block Diagram and Signal Flow Graph Q1
questions.question: A control system is shown in the Figure. Which option represents the correct transfer function of the system?
questions.explanation:
The given block diagram consists of a forward path and two feedback loops.
Method 1
Mason's Gain Formula: \(\dfrac{C(s)}{R(s)} = \frac{\sum P_k \Delta_k}{\Delta}\)
  • Forward Path (\(P_1\)): \[P_1 = \frac{1}{s+4}\]
  • Individual Loops (\(L_m\)): \[L_1 = \frac{1}{s+4} \times (-1) \times (-1) = \frac{1}{s+4} \quad ; \quad L_2 = \frac{1}{s+4} \times (+1) \times (-1) = -\frac{1}{s+4}\]
  • Determinant (\(\Delta\)): \[\Delta = 1 - (L_1 + L_2) = 1 - \left( \frac{1}{s+4} - \frac{1}{s+4} \right) = 1 - 0 = 1\]
  • Overall Transfer Function: \[\frac{C(s)}{R(s)} = \frac{P_1 \Delta_1}{\Delta} = \frac{\left( \frac{1}{s+4} \right) \cdot 1}{1} = \frac{1}{s+4}\]
Method 2
Block Diagram Reduction: Consider the error signal E(s) \[\boxed{\text{(B)} \ \ \frac{1}{s + 4}}\]
Key points
  • Mason's Gain Formula: \(\frac{C(s)}{R(s)} = \frac{\sum P_k \Delta_k}{\Delta}\)
    • \(P_k\): Gain of the \(k^{th}\) forward path
    • \(\Delta = 1 - (\text{sum of individual loop gains}) + (\text{sum of gain products of two non-touching loops}) - \dots\)
    • \(\Delta_k\): The cofactor of the \(k^{th}\) forward path, calculated by removing the loops touching the \(k^{th}\) path.

questions.question: Consider the unity negative feedback control system shown in the Figure. Value of gain \(K\) (\(>0\)) at which the given system will remain marginally stable is
questions.explanation:
For the system to be marginally stable, we analyze the characteristic equation: \[1 + G(s) = 0\] \[1 + \frac{K}{s(s + 7)(s + 11)} = 0\] \[s^3 + 18s^2 + 77s + K = 0\] Applying Routh-Hurwitz stability criterion for a third-order system \(as^3 + bs^2 + cs + d = 0\), the condition for marginal stability is: \[bc = ad\] \[18 \times 77 = 1 \times K_{\text{mar}}\] \[\boxed{K_{\text{mar}} = 1386}\]
Key points
Marginal stability occurs when a row in the Routh array becomes zero, leading to symmetric roots on the \(j\omega\) axis.

questions.question: For the control system shown in the Figure, the transfer function of a plant, \[G(s) = \frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)}\] is connected in cascade with a compensator \(C(s) = K\,(s+\alpha)\), where \(K\) and \(\alpha\) are positive real valued constants. Which of the following pairs \((K,\alpha)\) represent the correct values for the closed loop system to have poles at \((-3 \pm j\sqrt{5})\)?
questions.explanation: Given, \[G(s)=\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)}\] The compensator is \[C(s)=K(s+\alpha)\] For a unity feedback system, \[1+C(s)G(s)=0\] Substituting \(G(s)\) and \(C(s)\), \[1+\frac{K(s+\alpha)}{(s+1)(s+2)}=0\] Therefore, \[(s+1)(s+2)+K(s+\alpha)=0\] Expanding, \[s^2+3s+2+Ks+K\alpha=0\] \[s^2+(3+K)s+(2+K\alpha)=0\] The closed loop poles are given as \[-3\pm j\sqrt{5}\] Hence the characteristic equation becomes \[(s+3-j\sqrt{5})(s+3+j\sqrt{5})=0\] Using \[(a-b)(a+b)=a^2-b^2\] \[(s+3)^2+5=0\] \[s^2+6s+14=0\] Comparing coefficients, \[3+K=6\] \[K=3\] Also, \[2+K\alpha=14\] \[K\alpha=12\] Substituting \(K=3\), \[3\alpha=12\] \[\alpha=4\] \[\boxed{(B) ~3,4}\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: Let \(X\), \(N\), \(Y\) and \(Z\) be random variables. The variables \(X\) and \(N\) are independent of each other. \(X\) is uniformly distributed between \(-1\) and \(1\); \(N\) follows the Normal distribution with zero mean and unity variance. \(Y\) and \(Z\) are defined as, \(Y = X + N\) and \(Z = X^2 + N\). Which of the following pairs represents the values of correlation between \(X\) and \(Y\) and that between \(X\) and \(Z\)?
questions.explanation:
Given:
\[X \sim U(-1,1)\] Since \(X\) and \(N\) are independent, \(E[X]=E[N]=0\) and \[E[X^2]=\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{1}{3}\] for \(X\) uniformly distributed over \([-1,1]\). For \(Y=X+N\), \[E[XY]=E[X(X+N)] =E[X^2]+E[XN] =\frac{1}{3}+E[X]E[N] =\frac{1}{3}.\] For \(Z=X^2+N\), \[E[XZ]=E[X(X^2+N)] =E[X^3]+E[XN].\] Since \(X\) has a symmetric distribution about zero, \[E[X^3]=0, \qquad E[XN]=E[X]E[N]=0.\] Hence, \[E[XZ]=0.\] Therefore, the required pair is \[\boxed{\text{(A)}\ \dfrac{1}{3}\ \text{and}\ 0}\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: A wireless digital transmission scheme is using \(16\)-QAM over an additive white Gaussian noise channel and a maximum-likelihood receiver. Consider the information bit rate from source to be \(4\times10^6\) bits per second. The minimum transmission bandwidth (in MHz) of the modulated signal necessary for optimum recovery of information at the receiver is . (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation:
Given: \[\text{Modulation scheme} = 16\text{-QAM}\] \[R_b = 4\times10^6 \ \text{bits/s}\] Step 1: Find the Symbol Rate \(R_s\) Theory: In an \(M\)-ary digital modulation scheme, each symbol carries \[\log_2 M\]bits. Hence, the symbol rate is \[R_s=\frac{R_b}{\log_2 M}.\]For \(16\)-QAM, \[\log_2(16)=4.\]Therefore, \[R_s = \frac{R_b}{\log_2 M} = \frac{4\times10^6}{4} = 1\times10^6\]symbols/s. Step 2: Find the Minimum Transmission Bandwidth Theory: For ideal Nyquist signaling, the minimum transmission bandwidth is equal to the symbol rate. \[B_{\min}=R_s.\]Substituting the value of \(R_s\), \[B_{\min} = 1\times10^6 \ \text{Hz}\] \[\boxed{B_{\min}=1\ \text{MHz}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Bit Rate vs Symbol Rate: Do not assume \[R_s=R_b.\] For \(M\)-ary modulation, \[R_s=\frac{R_b}{\log_2 M}.\]
  • Bits per Symbol: For 16-QAM, \[\log_2(16)=4,\] not \(16\).
  • Units: The symbol rate is measured in baud (symbols/s), while the bit rate is measured in bits/s.
  • Bandwidth Conversion: Remember that \[10^6\ \text{Hz}=1\ \text{MHz}.\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: Consider a discrete memoryless source with an alphabet of four source symbols. \(s(t)\) is a multi-level \((-1,0,+1,+2)\) signal representing a long sequence of random symbols from the above source which is generating \(10^4\) symbols per second. Which of the following options is the correct value of equivalent Nyquist bandwidth of \(s(t)\)?
questions.explanation:
Given: A 4-level signal \[s(t)\in\{-1,0,+1,+2\}\]with symbol rate \[R_s = 10^4 \ \text{symbols/s}.\] Step 1: Determine the Equivalent Nyquist Bandwidth Theory: For a digital signal transmitted at a symbol rate \(R_s\), the minimum Nyquist bandwidth required for zero intersymbol interference (ISI) is \[B_{\text{Nyquist}} = \frac{R_s}{2}.\]The number of signal levels does not affect the Nyquist bandwidth; it depends only on the symbol rate. Substituting the given value, \[B_{\text{Nyquist}} = \frac{10^4}{2} = 5\times10^3 \ \text{Hz}.\] \[\boxed{B_{\text{Nyquist}}=5\ \text{kHz}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Confusing Bit Rate with Symbol Rate: The given rate is \[10^4 \ \text{symbols/s},\]not bits/s.
  • Using the Number of Levels: Do not multiply the bandwidth by 4 just because the signal has four levels.
  • Forgetting the Factor of 2: Nyquist bandwidth is \[\frac{R_s}{2},\] not \(R_s\).

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: A QPSK modulated signal from an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel is received with an \(E_b/N_0=8.4\) dB at the input of a coherent QPSK demodulator. A maximum-likelihood reception method is used in the demodulator. Assume the complementary error function \[\operatorname{erfc}(u)\cong \left[\frac{1}{u\sqrt{\pi}}\right]\exp(-u^2).\]Which is the nearest bit error rate (BER) at the output of the demodulator?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Convert \(\dfrac{E_b}{N_0}\) from dB to linear scale Theory: For BER calculations, the ratio \(\dfrac{E_b}{N_0}\) must first be converted from dB to its linear value. \[\frac{E_b}{N_0} = 10^{\frac{8.4}{10}} = 10^{0.84} \approx 6.92\]Therefore, \[\sqrt{\frac{E_b}{N_0}} = \sqrt{6.92} \approx 2.63\] Step 2: Use the given approximation Theory: For large values of \(u\), the complementary error function can be approximated as \[\operatorname{erfc}(u) \approx \frac{1}{u\sqrt{\pi}}\,e^{-u^2}\]Substituting \(u=2.63\), \[\operatorname{erfc}(2.63) \approx \frac{1}{2.63\sqrt{\pi}}\,e^{-(2.63)^2}\]Now, \[(2.63)^2 \approx 6.92\]and \[e^{-6.92} \approx 9.9\times10^{-4}\]Also, \[2.63\sqrt{\pi} \approx 2.63\times1.772 \approx 4.66\]Hence, \[\operatorname{erfc}(2.63) \approx \frac{9.9\times10^{-4}}{4.66} \approx 2.1\times10^{-4}\] Step 3: Compute the BER Theory: For QPSK, \[P_b = \frac{1}{2}\, \operatorname{erfc} \left( \sqrt{\frac{E_b}{N_0}} \right)\]Therefore, \[P_b = \frac{1}{2} \left(2.1\times10^{-4}\right)\] \[P_b \approx 1.05\times10^{-4}\]Thus, the nearest BER is \[\boxed{P_b \approx 10^{-4}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • QPSK BER Formula: Remember the correct BER expression: \[P_b = \frac{1}{2} \operatorname{erfc} \left( \sqrt{\frac{E_b}{N_0}} \right)\] Missing the factor \(\frac{1}{2}\) gives an answer twice the correct value.

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: The average bit error rate at the input of a \((7,4,1)\) Hamming decoder is \(0.10\). The probability that the decoder will fail to decode a received word correctly is . (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation: Given: \[p = 0.10\]where \(p\) is the average bit error probability at the input of the decoder. Theory: A Hamming \((7,4)\) code has minimum distance \[d_{\min}=3\]and hence can correct \[t=\left\lfloor \frac{d_{\min}-1}{2}\right\rfloor =1\]error per codeword. Therefore, decoding fails whenever two or more errors occur in a 7-bit codeword. Probability of Decoder Failure \[P(\text{failure}) = 1-P(0\ \text{errors})-P(1\ \text{error})\]For zero errors, \[P(0\ \text{errors}) = (1-p)^7 = (0.9)^7 = 0.4783\]For exactly one error, \[P(1\ \text{error}) = {}^7C_1\,p(1-p)^6 = 7p(1-p)^6\] \[= 7(0.1)(0.9)^6\] \[= 7(0.1)(0.5314) = 0.3720\]Hence, \[P(\text{failure}) = 1-0.4783-0.3720\] \[= 0.1497\] \[\boxed{P(\text{failure}) \approx 0.15}\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: Let the relevant bandwidth \(B\) of a digital communication system be \(1\,\text{MHz}\) and \[kT=-174\ \text{dBm/Hz},\]where \(k\) is Boltzmann's constant and \(T\) is the equivalent noise temperature of the receiver. The received signal power through an additive Gaussian channel is \(S=-80\ \text{dBm}.\) Which of the following statements are true about the Shannon capacity \(C\) of the channel?
questions.explanation:
Theory: Shannon's capacity for an AWGN channel is given by \[C=B\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR})\]where \(B\) is the channel bandwidth and \(\mathrm{SNR}\) is the signal-to-noise ratio. Given, \[B=1\,\text{MHz}=10^6\,\text{Hz}\] \[kT=-174\,\text{dBm/Hz}\] \[S=-80\,\text{dBm}\]Calculating the noise power \[N = kT+10\log_{10}(B)\] \[N = -174+10\log_{10}(10^6)\] \[N = -174+60 = -114\,\text{dBm}\]Calculating the signal-to-noise ratio \[\mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{dB}} = S-N\] \[= -80-(-114) = 34\,\text{dB}\]Converting into linear scale, \[\mathrm{SNR} = 10^{34/10} = 10^{3.4} \approx 2512\]Calculating the Shannon capacity \[C = B\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR})\] \[= 10^6\log_2(2513)\] \[= 10^6 \left( \frac{\ln(2513)}{\ln(2)} \right)\] \[\approx 10^6(11.3)\] \[C \approx 11.3\times10^6\ \text{bps}\] \[C \approx 11.3\,\text{Mbps} = 11.3B\]Hence, \[\boxed{\text{(C) } C>3B}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not use \(-174\,\text{dBm/Hz}\) directly as noise power. It is a noise power spectral density and must be multiplied by bandwidth.
  • Remember that \[1\,\text{MHz}=10^6\,\text{Hz}.\]
  • Convert SNR from dB to linear scale before applying Shannon's formula: \[\mathrm{SNR}=10^{\mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{dB}}/10}.\]
  • Use \[C=B\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}),\] not \(\log_{10}\).
  • Capacity is measured in bits/s, whereas bandwidth is measured in Hz.

questions.question: The electric field of a monochromatic plane wave travelling in a lossless isotropic and homogeneous medium is given by\[\vec{E}(z, t) = E_0[\hat{x}\cos(\omega t - kz) + \hat{y}\sin(\omega t - kz)]\]in a right-handed orthogonal co-ordinate system. Which of the following is the correct polarization of the electromagnetic wave?
questions.explanation: Given, \[\vec{E}(z, t) = E_0[\hat{x}\cos(\omega t - kz) + \hat{y}\sin(\omega t - kz)]\] [figure unavailable] At \(z = 0\): \[\vec{E}(t) = E_0 \cos \omega t \, \hat{a}_x + E_0 \sin \omega t \, \hat{a}_y\] As \(|E_{x0}| = |E_{y0}| = E_0\). Phase difference between \(E_x\) and \(E_y\) is: \[|\phi| = 90^\circ\] \(\therefore\) it is a circularly polarized wave. Now, at \(t = 0, \omega t = 0\), \(\vec{E} = E_0 \hat{a}_x\). At \(t = T/4, \omega t = \pi/2\), \(\vec{E} = E_0 \hat{a}_y\). With the right thumb in the direction of the wave propagation (\(\hat{a}_z\)), fingers curl in the direction of the electric field vector, hence it is Right-handed circularly polarized. \[\boxed{\text{(A) Right Handed Circularly Polarized}}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: Which option(s) represents/ represent the dielectric loss tangent of a substrate?
options: Ratio of the real to imaginary parts of the total displacement current
Ratio of the electric susceptibility to permittivity
Ratio of the polarization vector \(\vec{P}\) to the displacement vector \(\vec{D}\)
questions.explanation:
Under time-harmonic conditions, the total current density \(J\) in a dielectric is given by the sum of conduction current density \(J_{c}\) and displacement current density \(J_{d}\):\[J = \sigma E + j \omega \epsilon E\]Where \(\epsilon\) is the complex permittivity of the dielectric, defined as \(\epsilon = \epsilon' - j \epsilon''\). Substituting this into the equation for \(J\):\[J = \sigma E + j \omega E (\epsilon' - j \epsilon'')\]\[J = \sigma E + j \omega \epsilon' E + \omega \epsilon'' E\]Rearranging the terms into real and imaginary parts: \[J = (\sigma + \omega \epsilon'') E + j \omega \epsilon' E\] The loss tangent (\(\tan \delta\)) of the dielectric is defined by the ratio of the real part (dissipative component) to the imaginary part (reactive component) of the total current density: \[\tan \delta = \frac{\sigma + \omega \epsilon''}{\omega \epsilon'}\] Hence, the expressions leading to this ratio confirm that the relevant components are correctly identified. \[\boxed{(A, B):(\omega \epsilon'' + \sigma)/(\omega \epsilon')}\]
Key points
  • The total current density \(J\) is the sum of conduction current (\(J_{c} = \sigma E\)) and displacement current (\(J_{d} = \frac{\partial D}{\partial t} = j \omega \epsilon E\)).
  • Complex permittivity \(\epsilon = \epsilon' - j \epsilon''\) accounts for both energy storage (\(\epsilon'\)) and dielectric loss (\(\epsilon''\)).
  • Loss tangent \(\tan \delta\) represents the ratio of lossy power to lossless power in the medium.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse the real part of the complex permittivity (\(\epsilon'\)) with the imaginary part (\(\epsilon''\)) when calculating the ratio.
  • Ensure the \(j^{2} = -1\) substitution is performed correctly when expanding \(j \omega E (-j \epsilon'')\).

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: A complex load (in \(\Omega\)) is represented as \(\Gamma_{L} = 0.5 \angle 30^{\circ}\) on the Smith chart. A co-axial cable with a characteristic impedance of \(50\,\Omega\) is connected to the load. The new input impedance of the load now moves to a diametrically opposite point on the same \(\Gamma\) circle on the Smith chart. Which option is the nearest input impedance of the cable connected load (in \(\Omega\))?
questions.explanation:
Given that the initial reflection coefficient is \(\Gamma_{L} = 0.5 \angle 30^{\circ}\) and the characteristic impedance of the line is \(Z_{0} = 50\,\Omega\). Moving to a diametrically opposite point on the Smith chart corresponds to a phase shift of \(180^{\circ}\). The new reflection coefficient, \(\Gamma_{L,new}\), is given by: \[\Gamma_{L,new} = 0.5 \angle (30^{\circ} + 180^{\circ}) = 0.5 \angle 210^{\circ} = 0.5 \angle -150^{\circ}\] The input impedance \(Z_{in}\) is calculated using the transmission line impedance transformation formula: \[Z_{in} = Z_{0} \left[ \frac{1 + \Gamma_{L,new}}{1 - \Gamma_{L,new}} \right]\] Substituting the given values: \[Z_{in} = 50 \left[ \frac{1 + 0.5 \angle -150^{\circ}}{1 - 0.5 \angle -150^{\circ}} \right]\] Using \(0.5 \angle -150^{\circ} = 0.5(\cos(-150^{\circ}) + j\sin(-150^{\circ})) \approx -0.433 - j0.25\): \[Z_{in} = 50 \left[ \frac{1 + (-0.433 - j0.25)}{1 - (-0.433 - j0.25)} \right]\] \[Z_{in} = 50 \left[ \frac{0.567 - j0.25}{1.433 + j0.25} \right]\] Converting to polar form for division: \[Z_{in} = 50 \times 0.426 \angle -33.7^{\circ}\] \[Z_{in} \approx 21.3 \angle -33.7^{\circ}\,\Omega\] Converting to rectangular form: \[Z_{in} = 17.72 - j11.82\,\Omega\] \[\boxed{(B):17.72 - j11.82\,\Omega}\]
Key points
  • Moving to a diametrically opposite point on a Smith chart represents a transformation through a quarter-wavelength section, effectively adding \(180^{\circ}\) to the phase of \(\Gamma_{L}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • When using the Smith chart for this transformation, remember that the magnitude \(|\Gamma|\) remains constant, but the phase shifts by exactly \(\pm 180^{\circ}\).

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: For a lossless passive two-port network, \(|S_{11}|\) and \(|S_{21}|\) intersect at \(-3\text{ dB}\). For a lossy passive two-port network, \(|S_{11}|\) and \(|S_{21}|\) intersect at \(-4\text{ dB}\). The percentage of power dissipated in the lossy network at the intersection frequency is (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation:
For a lossy passive two-port network, the conservation of energy dictates that the total input power \(P_{in}\) is the sum of the reflected power, transmitted power, and the power dissipated within the network (\(P_{loss}\)): \[P_{in} = |S_{11}|^{2}P_{in} + |S_{21}|^{2}P_{in} + P_{loss}\] Dividing the entire equation by \(P_{in}\), we get: \[1 = |S_{11}|^{2} + |S_{21}|^{2} + \frac{P_{loss}}{P_{in}}\] Given \(|S_{11}| = |S_{21}| = -4\,\text{dB}\), we first convert these values from decibels to linear scale: \[20 \log_{10} |S_{11}| = -4\] \[\log_{10} |S_{11}| = -0.2\] \[|S_{11}| = 10^{-0.2}\] Squaring both sides to find the power coefficients: \[|S_{11}|^{2} = |S_{21}|^{2} = (10^{-0.2})^{2} = 10^{-0.4} \approx 0.3981\] Now, substitute these values into the power balance equation: \[1 = 0.3981 + 0.3981 + \frac{P_{loss}}{P_{in}}\] \[1 = 0.7962 + \frac{P_{loss}}{P_{in}}\] \[\frac{P_{loss}}{P_{in}} = 1 - 0.7962 = 0.2038\] Expressing the dissipated power as a percentage: \[\%\frac{P_{loss}}{P_{in}} = 20.38\%\] \[\boxed{20.38\%}\]
Key points
  • For a passive network, the sum of the squares of the magnitudes of the scattering parameters in a column must be less than or equal to 1.
  • Lossy networks dissipate energy as heat, represented by the term \(\frac{P_{loss}}{P_{in}} = 1 - \sum |S_{ij}|^2\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse power ratios (which use \(10\log_{10}\)) with voltage/field ratios (which use \(20\log_{10}\)) when converting from dB.

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: The cutoff frequency (in GHz) for the dominant \(\text{TE}_{10}\) mode of an air-filled rectangular waveguide of inner dimension \(0.28\text{ inch} \times 0.14\text{ inch}\) is (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
The general formula for the cut-off frequency \(f_{c}\) of a \(TE_{mn}\) mode in a rectangular waveguide is given by: \[f_{c, TE_{mn}} = \frac{c}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{m}{a}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{n}{b}\right)^{2}}\] For the dominant \(TE_{10}\) mode, where \(m=1\) and \(n=0\), the expression simplifies to: \[f_{c, TE_{10}} = \frac{c}{2a}\] Given that the waveguide dimensions are in inches, we convert the width \(a\) to centimeters using the factor \(1\,\text{inch} = 2.54\,\text{cm}\). Assuming the standard waveguide dimension \(a = 0.28\,\text{inch}\): \[a = 0.28 \times 2.54\,\text{cm} = 0.7112\,\text{cm} = 0.7112 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\] Using the speed of light \(c = 3 \times 10^{10}\,\text{cm/s}\): \[f_{c, TE_{10}} = \frac{3 \times 10^{10}}{2 \times 0.28 \times 2.54} = \frac{3 \times 10^{10}}{1.4224} \approx 21.09 \times 10^{9}\,\text{Hz}\] \[\boxed{21.09\,\text{GHz}}\]
Key points
  • The \(TE_{10}\) mode is the dominant mode in a rectangular waveguide, having the lowest cut-off frequency.
  • The cut-off frequency depends inversely on the dimension \(a\) for the \(TE_{10}\) mode.
  • Always ensure consistent units (e.g., converting inches to cm or meters) before performing calculations with \(c\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Forgetting to convert the dimension given in inches to centimeters or meters, leading to an incorrect result by a factor of 2.54.

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: Consider the Friis' transmission equation,\[P_R = \dfrac{P_T G_T G_R \lambda^2}{(4\pi D)^2}\]where \(P_R\) and \(P_T\) are the received and the transmitted powers, respectively. \(G_T\) and \(G_R\) are the gain of transmitting and receiving antennas, respectively, \(D\) is the distance between the transmitting and receiving antennas, and \(\lambda\) is the wavelength in free space. Given: \(G_T = G_R = 1.0\), \(\lambda = 0.30 \text{ m}\) and \(P_T = +10 \text{ dBm}\). Choose the distance (\(D\)), in km, from the following options at which the received power, \(P_R = -90 \text{ dBm}\)?
questions.explanation:
Given data: \[G_t = G_r = 1\] \[\lambda = 0.30\,\text{m}\] \[P_t = 10\,\text{dBm}\] \[P_r = -90\,\text{dBm}\] From Friis' transmission formula, the received power \(P_r\) is given by: \[P_r = \frac{P_t G_t G_r}{\left( \frac{4 \pi D}{\lambda} \right)^2}\] First, convert the power values from \(\text{dBm}\) to Watts (\(\text{W}\)): \[P_r|_{\text{dBm}} = 10 \log_{10} \left( \frac{P_r}{1\,\text{mW}} \right) \implies -90 = 10 \log_{10} \left( \frac{P_r}{1 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{W}} \right)\] \[\frac{P_r}{10^{-3}} = 10^{-9} \implies P_r = 10^{-12}\,\text{W}\] \[P_t|_{\text{dBm}} = 10 \log_{10} \left( \frac{P_t}{1\,\text{mW}} \right) \implies 10 = 10 \log_{10} \left( \frac{P_t}{10^{-3}\,\text{W}} \right)\] \[\frac{P_t}{10^{-3}} = 10^1 \implies P_t = 0.01\,\text{W}\] Rearranging the Friis' formula to solve for distance \(D\): \[\left( \frac{4 \pi D}{\lambda} \right)^2 = \frac{P_t G_t G_r}{P_r}\] \[D = \frac{\lambda}{4 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{P_t G_t G_r}{P_r}}\] Substituting the values: \[D = \frac{0.30}{4 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{0.01 \times 1 \times 1}{1 \times 10^{-12}}}\] \[D = \frac{0.30}{4 \pi} \sqrt{0.01 \times 10^{12}} = \frac{0.30}{4 \pi} \sqrt{10^{10}}\] \[D = \frac{0.30}{4 \pi} \times 10^5 = \frac{0.15}{2 \pi} \times 10^5\,\text{m}\] \[D = \frac{15000}{2 \pi}\,\text{m} = \frac{15}{2 \pi}\,\text{km}\] \[\boxed{(B):\frac{15}{2 \pi}}\]
Key points
  • \(P_r|_{\text{dBm}} = 10 \log_{10} \left( \frac{P_r}{1\,\text{mW}} \right)\)
  • Ensure all power units are converted from \(\text{dBm}\) or \(\text{dBW}\) to linear Watts before substitution into the power ratio formula.
  • Distance \(D\) must be in the same unit system as \(\lambda\) (meters).

questions.question: Exacerbate : Mitigate :: ________ Choose the option with the correct pair of words to fill the blank.
questions.explanation:
We need to find the word pair whose relationship mirrors the baseline analogy *Exacerbate : Mitigate*. Let us define the core semantic relationship linking these two verbs:
  • Exacerbate: To make a problem worse, more severe, or to intensify a negative state.
  • Mitigate: To make a problem less severe, serious, or to alleviate a negative state.
The baseline relationship follows an **antonym pair** structure where both words operate along the same scalar dimension (the severity or intensity of a problem). We evaluate each option against this exact framework:
  • Option A (Aggravate : Alleviate): *Aggravate* means to worsen or intensify a problem (synonymous with *exacerbate*), while *alleviate* means to make a problem less severe or relieve it (synonymous with *mitigate*). This perfectly replicates the antonym relationship along the identical semantic axis.
  • Option B and C: *Precipitate* means to cause something to happen suddenly or prematurely, which fails to track the direct antonym axis of *mitigate*.
  • Option D (Emancipate : Exonerate): Both words carry distinct positive legal meanings (*emancipate* means to set free; *exonerate* means to absolve from blame), meaning they are not antonyms.
Therefore, Option A is the uniquely correct parallel pair. \[\boxed{\text{A. Aggravate : Alleviate}}\]
Key points
  • The relationship is a parallel matching antonym set: \(\text{Exacerbate} \approx \text{Aggravate}\) and \(\text{Mitigate} \approx \text{Alleviate}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Avoid selecting pairs based solely on generic positive or negative connotations; the target choice must mirror the precise action-oriented antonym axis of the prompt.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Four people P, Q, R, and S, of different ages, make the following observations. P -- I am younger than S. Q -- I am neither the youngest nor the oldest. R -- P is older than me. Based on these observations, the youngest person is _____.
questions.explanation:
From the given logical statements, we need to determine who is the youngest individual among P, Q, R, and S. We break down the relational constraints and inequalities from each statement (where higher value indicates older age):
  1. P's Statement: \(P < S\) (P is younger than S).
  2. R's Statement: \(R < P\) (R is younger than P).
  3. Chaining the Inequalities: Combining these two structural relations gives the ordering chain: \[R < P < S\]
  4. Q's Statement: Q states that he is neither the youngest (\(\min\)) nor the oldest (\(\max\)).
Let us analyze where Q can be placed within the established chain \(R < P < S\). Since Q cannot be the absolute youngest or oldest, Q cannot be placed to the left of R or to the right of S. Q must fit somewhere within the internal bounds of the sequence, meaning \(R < Q\) and \(Q < S\). Regardless of whether Q is older or younger than P, R remains bounded at the absolute minimum position of the ordering chain under all valid permutations. Therefore, R is strictly the youngest individual. This logical derivation matches Option C. \[\boxed{\text{C. R}}\]
Key points
  • Chaining linear inequalities allows you to establish definitive minimum and maximum boundary elements across a dataset.
  • Boundary constraints like ``neither min nor max'' eliminate items from extreme positions without needing to fix their exact internal rank.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not waste time trying to find the exact relative age rank between P and Q; their internal positioning has no mathematical effect on identifying the absolute minimum boundary element.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: ``He often _______ the numbers. False claims are not going to help. Honesty _______ trust'', said the manager. Choose the option with the correct order of words to fill the blanks.
questions.explanation:

An analysis of the first sentence segment, ``He often the numbers. False claims are not going to help,'' indicates that the individual alters or inflates numeric values, as established by the negative context of ``false claims.'' The verb exaggerates fits this meaning directly. Looking at the second sentence segment, ``Honesty trust,'' the statement expresses a foundational principle where being honest acts as a structural catalyst that creates or gives rise to trust. The verb engenders means precisely to cause, produce, or give rise to a feeling or situation. Evaluating the alternatives:
  • Option A (exaggerates; engenders): Fits both contextual positions perfectly.
  • Option B (excels; encourages): The phrase ``excels the numbers'' is grammatically incorrect.
  • Option C (aggravates; alleviates): ``Aggravates the numbers'' does not fit the semantic context.
  • Option D (diminishes; eliminates): Contradicts the sentence logic because honesty does not eliminate trust.
Hence, Option A is the uniquely consistent choice. \[\boxed{\text{A. exaggerates; engenders}}\]
Key points
  • Exaggerate means to represent something as being larger, greater, or better than it really is.
  • Engender is a precise verb signifying to cause or breed a specific systemic condition.

We need to find the pair of words \((P, Q)\) that satisfies the double analogy relation: \[\text{Charity} : P :: \text{Retaliation} : Q\] Establishing the core semantic relationships links a specific human behavior to its motivating character trait. Charity is an action driven by someone who is defined as magnanimous (generous, kind, and forgiving). Parallel to this, retaliation is an action driven by someone who is defined as vindictive (vengeful, spiteful, and seeking revenge). Testing the alternatives shows that Option A is incorrect because *parsimonious* means stingy, which is the opposite of charity. Option B is incorrect because *amicable* means friendly, which contradicts retaliation. Option C is incorrect because *resentful* is a temporary emotion rather than a character trait that matches the structural setup. Therefore, **Option D** (\(P = \text{Magnanimous}; \ Q = \text{Vindictive}\)) is the only pair that completes the parallel analogy layout. \[\boxed{\text{D. P = Magnanimous; Q = Vindictive}}\]
Key points
  • The analogy maps an action to its defining character trait: \(\text{[Action]} : \text{[Adjective describing the actor]}\).

Conversely, an antagonist is a person who actively opposes or is hostile to someone or something; in literature, it represents the principal adversary of the protagonist. Evaluating the remaining options:
  • Aagnostic: A person who believes that nothing is known or can be known of the existence or nature of God.
  • Carsonist: A person who deliberately sets fire to property.
  • Danarchist: A person who rebels against any authority, established order, or ruling power.
Hence, Option B is the direct antonym. \[\boxed{\text{B. antagonist}}\]
Key points
  • Protagonist (Greek prōtagōnistēs: first actor) and Antagonist (Greek antagōnistēs: competitor/opponent) form a classic literary antonym pair based on opposing Greek prefixes.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: `When the teacher is in the room, all students stand silently.' If the above statement is true, which one of the following statements is not necessarily true?
options: If any student is not standing silently, then the teacher is not in the room.
When the teacher is in the room, all students are silent.
If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room.
When the teacher is in the room, all students are standing.
questions.explanation:
Given the true conditional premise: ``When the teacher is in the room, all students stand silently,'' we need to identify which statement is not necessarily true. Let us express the prompt statement in standard propositional logic notation: * Let \(P\) = The teacher is in the room. * Let \(Q\) = All students stand silently. The premise states that \(P \implies Q\) is **True**. Let us analyze the logical validity of each option:
  • Option A: ``If any student is not standing silently, then the teacher is not in the room.'' This translates to \( eg Q \implies eg P\), which is the **contrapositive** of our premise. A contrapositive is always logically equivalent to the original implication statement, so this is strictly True.
  • Option B: ``When the teacher is in the room, all students are silent.'' This is a restatement of \(P \implies Q\), which is explicitly True.
  • Option C: ``If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room.'' This translates to \(Q \implies P\), which is the **converse** of our premise. The truth of an implication does not guarantee the truth of its converse (affirming the consequent). Thus, this is not necessarily true.
  • Option D: ``When the teacher is in the room, all students are standing.'' This is a valid direct restatement of the conditional premise, so it is strictly True.
Hence, Option C is not necessarily true. \[ oxed{ ext{ C. If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room.}}\]
Key points
  • Given a true implication \(P \implies Q\), its contrapositive (\( eg Q \implies eg P\)) is guaranteed to be true, while its converse (\(Q \implies P\)) and inverse (\( eg P \implies eg Q\)) are logical fallacies and not necessarily true.

questions.question:
Combinatorics deals with problems involving counting. For example, ``How many distinct arrangements of N distinct objects in M spaces on a circle are possible?'' is a typical problem in combinatorics. This kind of counting is sometimes used in the modeling of several physical phenomena. Often, in such models, the different combinatorial possibilities are assigned probability values. Assigning probabilities enables the computation of the average values of physical quantities. Consider the following statements:
  • P: Combinatorics is always invoked in the modeling of physical phenomena.
  • Q: Modeling some physical phenomena involves assigning probabilities to combinatorial possibilities in order to compute average values of physical quantities.
Based on the passage above, what can be inferred about statements P and Q?
options: P is False and Q is False
P is False and Q is True
P is True and Q is False
P is True and Q is True
questions.explanation:
Based on the text passage regarding combinatorics and physical modeling, we need to determine the truth values of statements P and Q. Let us analyze the text to evaluate each statement:
  • Statement P: ``Combinatorics is always invoked in the modeling of physical phenomena.'' The text states that combinatorics is ``sometimes used in the modeling of several physical phenomena.'' The absolute qualifier **always** in statement P overextends this claim, making statement P **False**.
  • Statement Q: ``Modeling some physical phenomena involves assigning probabilities to combinatorial possibilities in order to compute average values of physical quantities.'' The text explicitly notes: ``Often, in such models, the different combinatorial possibilities are assigned probability values. Assigning probabilities enables the computation of the average values of physical quantities.'' This matches statement Q directly, making it **True**.
Therefore, P is False and Q is True, which corresponds to Option B. \[\boxed{\text{ B. P is False and Q is True}}\]
Key points
  • Critical reading requires distinguishing between absolute constraints (e.g., *always*, *must*) and partial conditions (e.g., *sometimes*, *often*) mentioned in text passages.

Accelerate also means to cause something to move faster or happen sooner, matching the synonym series perfectly. The remaining choices are contextually incorrect: Retard means to delay or slow down, Provide means to supply or make available, and Disable means to incapacitate. \[\boxed{\text{A. Accelerate}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: `When it is raining, peacocks dance.' Based only on this sentence, which one of the following options is necessarily true?
options: Peacocks dance only when it is raining.
When peacocks dance, it is raining.
When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.
When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance.
questions.explanation:
Given the conditional premise statement: ``When it is raining, peacocks dance,'' we need to identify which statement is necessarily true. Let us express the premise statement using propositional logic operators: * Let \(R\) = It is raining. * Let \(D\) = Peacocks dance. The prompt statement means that the implication \(R \implies D\) is **True**. Let us analyze the logical validity of the choices:
  • Choice A: ``Peacocks dance only when it is raining.'' This maps to \(D \implies R\) (the converse), which is a logical fallacy and not necessarily true.
  • Choice B: ``When peacocks dance, it is raining.'' This is another restatement of the converse \(D \implies R\), which is not necessarily true.
  • Choice C: ``When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.'' This translates directly to \( eg D \implies eg R\), which is the **contrapositive** of our premise. Since a conditional statement and its contrapositive are always logically equivalent, this statement is strictly True.
  • Choice D: ``When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance.'' This maps to \( eg R \implies eg D\) (the inverse), which is not necessarily true.
\[ oxed{ ext{C. When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.}}\]
Key points
  • For any fundamentally true implication \(P \implies Q\), its conditional contrapositive (\( eg Q \implies eg P\)) is always logically guaranteed to be true.

Setting \(P = \text{Thirst}\) and \(Q = \text{Hunger}\) creates a perfectly balanced double analogy along identical biological axes. \[\boxed{\text{A. P = Thirst; Q = Hunger}}\]

Unfortunately, he got out without scoring any runs. Hence, there won't be any change in the captaincy for now.' Based on the paragraph above, which one of the following statements is true?

The current captain is older than Anish.
Anish is the youngest player in his team.
questions.explanation:
